1) The general partitioning scheme is give / 30-50 GB and give the rest to /home. By doing it this way, you can install other distros on top of / and your /home partition will be untouched, allowing you to keep all your data.

There are other directories you may want on their own partition like /tmp and /opt, but you don't have to worry about them for now.

2) You have two graphic driver options because there are two different drivers, an open source driver and proprietary driver. Since you have an nVidia chipset, stick with the proprietary driver. If you had AMD I would suggest the open source one.

3) I hate WINE. A lot of people claim to have great use out of it but every single time I do a litmus test it always fails. There are a couple examples that worked well, but I don't rely on WINE for my entertainment. I have enough native games that those few Windows titles I can do without.

Not to mention, the game developers could release an update which breaks WINE. We saw this with Steam last week. Valve pushed an update which would crash on startup if you used WINE. Granted, a fix was made pretty quickly (few days later), that level of regression and without a proper support stream makes it quite retarded to have to rely on it for your gaming needs.

In my experience, Linux is far simpler, after you have taken some time to sit back and study how the disparate parts of the OS go together to make a working system.

Also, unlike with Windows, Linux error outputs by an' large are written in English and give you solid keywords you can use to search for solutions.

Linux also has a large community behind it on a number of distros that actually know what they are doing. Contrast this with so-called Windows Gurus who really don't truly understand how their OS works, beyond memorizing KB articles and common troubleshooting steps. You will rarely, if ever, see someone with Linux knowledge advising you to reformat to fix an issue. You can always recover a damaged Linux installation, either by using the shell or chroot. You just need to decide if it is worth the time for the reward.

As for your questions:

  1. Look into making a swap file, rather than a swap partition. You can think of this as similar to Windows' paging file.

  2. With Nvidia, I'd recommend installing the nvidia-340x one. The open source drivers aren't there yet, for Nvidia GPUs.

  3. There is nothing wrong with using WINE, it is perfectly fine. I have plenty of games configured to run in WINE. No problem. You can use GUI frontends such as PlayOnLinux to manage installation of games/programs via WINE. I would suggest you read up on how WINE works, first of all, to ensure you have the best experience.
